case_name: Joseph v. Concordia Student Union Inc.
text:
JH-5108

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-05-075594-026

DATE:

FEBRUARY 20, 2003

______________________________________________________________________

PRESENT:

THE HONOURABLE

MR. JUSTICE ALLAN R. HILTON

______________________________________________________________________

NOAH JOSEPH, NOAH SARNA, DAN
HADAD, NAOMI SARNA, LAURA SONEGO, PATRICK AMAR, SHARON KOIFMAN, ADAM SPIRO,
EDNA ARGALGI AND ARIANE DRAY

Plaintiffs

v.

CONCORDIA STUDENT UNION INC.

Defendant

and

CONCORDIA
UNIVERSITY

Mise en cause

and

CONGRÈS JUIF
CANADIEN/CANADIAN JEWISH CONGRESS

Intervenant

______________________________________________________________________

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT
[1]

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The political turmoil that haunts the Middle
East is at the heart of this action that pits 10 students of the Jewish faith
against the Concordia Student Union and Concordia University. All of the
plaintiffs are members of a student club known as Concordia Hillel, and eight
of them hold executive positions. Hillel is described as an organization
"whose objectives are to promote, preserve and defend Jewish cultural,
spiritual and social activities at the University and to advocate, on behalf of
Concordia Jewish students, issues of concern to Jewish students at the
University".

[
2
]

As a result of the C.S.U. having adopted
resolutions on December 2 and December 12, 2002 which the
plaintiffs contend, amongst other effects, ban and disenfranchise Hillel as a
student club as well as suspend its funding, the plaintiffs have initiated
proceedings that seek orders of injunction, declaratory relief and damages that
may be summarized as follows:

A)        Against
the C.S.U.

•

to declare the two resolutions without effect
and ordering the reinstatement of Hillel;

•

to order the C.S.U. and its officers to respect
its constitution and to conform to the University's rules, regulations and
policies;

•

to order that the funds to finance Hillel be
placed in trust for the 2002 – 2003 academic year;

•

to condemn the C.S.U. to pay the plaintiffs
$100,000 as punitive damages as well as all of their extra-judicial fees in the
present case.

B)        Against
the University

•

to order it to enforce its various rules,
regulations and policies concerning respect of students and civil, peaceful
debate;

•

to order it to enforce its authority over its
campus and facilities so as to prevent their illegal or improper use.

[
3
]

Apart from allegations that relate directly to
what the plaintiffs describe as the offending resolutions adopted by the
C.S.U., the plaintiffs also devote several paragraphs in their action to
allegations that assert that the C.S.U. is dominated by persons who are not
only extremists, anarchists and anti-capitalists, but who also virulently
oppose the State of Israel  as well as seeking to discredit and de-legitimatize
the State of Israel and its student supporters at Concordia. Considerable
emphasis is also placed on what is described as a riot at the University last
September which resulted in the cancellation of a speech that was to be given
at Concordia by a former Prime Minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, in which
it is said that several members of the C.S.U. executive and Council of
Representatives participated with the object of preventing Mr. Netanyahu from
speaking. In addition, the plaintiffs allege what follows in paragraph 15 of
their Declaration:

“In pursuance of its agenda and
policies, the C.S.U. has consistently opposed any rational, civil debate on the
various points of view concerning the politics and relationships of the peoples
and inhabitants of the Middle East. The C.S.U. has consistently attempted to
promote and only permit the hearing of the voice of persons opposed to the
State of Israel. The C.S.U. has consistently attempted to diminish and where
possible silence the voice of persons who support the State of Israel. This
agenda and policy has in turn had a direct and immediate impact on Jewish
students at the University who find themselves increasingly subject to
anti-Israel and anti-Jewish propaganda and harassment either issued by the
C.S.U., promoted by the C.S.U. or issued and promoted by clubs and
organizations sponsored by the C.S.U.”

[
4
]

The plaintiffs also complain about what they
consider to be the University’s indifference to their plight by its alleged
failure “to take control of its campus”, and “to assert its authority over its
facilities and university life”.

[
5
]

The resolutions adopted by the C.S.U. that the
plaintiffs seek to annul were driven by the C.S.U. Council of Representatives'
belief that Hillel had authorized the distribution of a leaflet that solicited
volunteers from outside Israel to join the Israeli Defence Forces. The
plaintiffs set forth a variety of grounds to have the resolutions annulled, not
the least of which is the fact that Hillel did not authorise the distribution
of the leaflet, and that it was never given notice that the resolutions would
be considered. As a result, they say Hillel was deprived of an opportunity to
present its position.

[
6
]

Given the context in which they were adopted, as
referred to in paragraphs [3] and [4] above, the plaintiffs contend that the
two resolutions were the proverbial straw that broke the camel’s back.

[
7
]

The C.S.U. and the University have yet to file
any responsive pleadings to the action, and the plaintiffs have just recently
initiated interlocutory injunction proceedings.

[
8
]

It is in this factual and procedural context
that the Court was asked to receive an aggressive intervention presented by the
Canadian Jewish Congress, an organization that has been in existence since 1919
and which has, amongst its objects, acting in matters that affect the Canadian
Jewish community and the Jewish people in the State of Israel, as well as
investigating and devising means to overcome anti-Semitism in Canada. Alleging
that over the past two years it has become aware of what it describes as a
highly problematic situation for Jewish students attending Concordia, including
an atmosphere of intimidation perpetuated in large part by the C.S.U., the
C.J.C. not only supports the plaintiffs' position, but also requests the
issuance of various declarations and orders that may be summarized as follows:

A)        Against
the C.S.U.

•

to order it to issue an apology to the Jewish
community in Canada for illegally banning Hillel at Concordia, thereby causing
great anxiety within the Canadian Jewish community;

•

to order it to cease the harassment of Jewish
students and Jewish organizations on campus;

•

to order it to abide by its own by-laws and
regulations, and to repeal the resolutions adopted last December respecting
Hillel;

•

to order it to pay symbolic moral damages of
$1.00 and all of its extra-judicial fees.

B)       Against the University

•

to declare it legally and morally obligated to
provide an appropriate learning environment on its campus and to ensure the
safety and welfare of all of its students that is free of discrimination and
harassment;

•

to order it to revoke the two C.S.U.
resolutions;

•

to order it to enforce its existing  rules and
regulations or to adopt other ones so as to ensure an appropriate environment
on campus for all students, including those of the Jewish faith.

[
9
]

The C.J.C. expresses a great deal of concern
about what it describes as an atmosphere of intimidation and hostility toward
Jewish students at Concordia which it says has been perpetuated in large
measure by the C.S.U. through some of its officers and members. It notes that
the incident involving Mr. Netanyahu received widespread publicity around the
world, and included reports to the effect that Jewish students were spat at and
had pennies thrown at their feet. It also observes that the subsequent
resolutions of the C.S.U. concerning Hillel “caused great trepidation again to
the Canadian Jewish community and confirmed in their collective consciousness
that the University has become an unfriendly and indeed hostile place to be
insofar as Jewish students were concerned”.

[
10
]

The plaintiffs welcome the prospect of the
intervention by the C.J.C., and point out that it has the kind of expert
experience and resources in matters affecting the Jewish community in Canada
that situate it ideally to participate in the proceedings. The C.S.U. contests
the reception of the intervention, largely on the basis that the dispute between
the plaintiffs and the C.S.U. is a private one to which developing case law
concerning interventions in public law or public issue disputes does not apply.
The University takes no position on whether the C.J.C. should be permitted to
participate in the proceedings.

[
11
]

Clearly, the strict approach to the reception of
interventions has been relaxed considerably in cases involving federal and
provincial human rights legislation, as well as the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
. A classic illustration is the judgment of Grenier,
J. in
Rothman's, Benson & Hedges v. The Attorney General of Canada
,
[2]
where after enunciating seven criteria a
court should examine in order to determine whether an intervention in a public
law or constitutional cases should be received, she said this:

"Le pouvoir discrétionnaire
des tribunaux en pareille matière vise essentiellement à assurer que le tiers
qui demande d'intervenir pourra apporter une contribution appréciable dans la
solution du litige tout en s'assurant que l'intervention n'aura pas pour effet
de dissiper les ressources judiciaires en allongeant inutilement le débat. Afin
de déterminer si la demande d'intervention est justifiée, le Tribunal doit donc
évaluer la situation en soupesant les avantages et les inconvénients.

"Il faut donc répondre à la
question suivante: l'intérêt de la justice sera-t-il mieux servi si la demande
d'intervention est accueillie? Il s'agit en quelque sorte de déterminer si les
avantages qui pourront procurer l'intervention sont plus importants que les
inconvénients qui y sont rattachés. Tel que le soulignait Lavine dans une
article intitulé «Advocating Values: Public Interest Intervention in
Charter

litigation», le test est le suivant:

In applying both
the directly affected criterion in the public interest standing test and the
unique and different perspective criterion in public interest intervention
applications, the Court is required to weigh the value of public participation
against the preservation of judicial resources
."
[3]

[
12
]

Grenier, J. went on to note that the proposed
intervenants before her had what she described as a real interest in one of the
issues that would be argued in the case on the merits relating to whether the
impugned provisions of the
Tobacco Act
[4]
satisfied the criteria of
section 1
of the
Canadian
Charter
. That being said, she received the intervention of only one of
the proposed intervenants, and circumscribed its role in the conduct of the
litigation.
[5]

[
13
]

The C.S.U. argues that in reality, this case is
nothing more than a private dispute between it and the plaintiffs that is
governed by the applicable provisions of its General By-laws, its Student Clubs
Manual, the University’s policy on the recognition of student organizations and
the use of university space, as well as the provincial statute under which the
C.S.U. obtained accreditation as a student union.
[6]
Accordingly, the C.S.U. contends that the
more relaxed approach to the reception of interventions in cases involving
constitutional law or other areas of public law is not warranted insofar as the
proposed intervention of the C.J.C. is concerned, and that the Court should
therefore follow the more traditional approach requiring a personal, real and
direct interest in the outcome of the case.
[7]

By way of analogy, since the C.J.C. wishes to intervene in a pending case
rather than initiate its own case, the C.S.U. also relies on the proposition
that even in delictual matters that assert a claim based on fundamental
freedoms, a plaintiff must still have a direct and personal interest rather
than one that is more general in nature.
[8]

[
14
]

There is no doubt that once this case reaches a
hearing, whether on the merits or for interlocutory relief, the C.S.U. will
rely on the instruments described in paragraph [13] above and others of a similar
nature to defend its position. It is also reasonable to assume, based on its
submission in the present matter, that the C.S.U. will contend that the context
of harassment described by the plaintiffs in their proceedings is essentially
irrelevant to the relief they seek.

[
15
]

Despite the very able presentation of counsel
for the C.S.U., however, the Court cannot ignore the context of ongoing
harassment and intimidation in which the plaintiffs say the so-called offending
resolutions relating to Hillel were adopted. It is precisely in that context
that the C.J.C. has a genuine interest, and would be of some assistance in the
resolution of the plaintiffs’ claim. On balance, the Court considers that the
presence of the C.J.C. would be valuable, and if adequately narrowed, would not
unduly prolong the trial on the merits or the hearing for an interlocutory
injunction, nor dissipate judicial resources.

[
16
]

The conclusions sought by the C.J.C., however,
go far beyond what is appropriate as an aggressive intervention. Many of them
state, in different words, what the plaintiffs seek, and others, such as the
order that the C.S.U. be required to issue an apology to the Jewish community
in Canada, or be condemned to pay symbolic damages, are of doubtful legality,
or are improbably justiciable.

[
17
]

For these reasons, at the conclusion of the
hearing, and in the exercise of its recognized discretion, the Court rendered
judgment in the following terms:

[
18
]

RECEIVES
the
intervention of the Canadian Jewish Congress for the limited purpose only of
establishing the effect on the Jewish community in Canada of the incidents and
events described in the plaintiffs’ declaration;

[
19
]

ORDERS
the
Canadian Jewish Congress, on or before February 28, 2003, to serve and file an
amended intervention which contains conclusions asking that its intervention be
maintained with costs and that the action of the plaintiffs be maintained in
accordance with its conclusions;

[
20
]

RESERVES
to any
judge of this Court hearing any matter in this case the authority to:

A)     limit the number of witnesses that counsel for the Canadian
Jewish Congress may call and the duration of the examination in chief;

B)     limit the extent to which, if any, such counsel may also
examine witnesses called by the plaintiffs, or cross-examine witnesses called
by the other two parties;

C)     establish the duration of oral argument to be made by such
counsel, with costs to follow suit.
